reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: The commonest cause of primary hyperparathyroidism is a single hyperfunctioning adenoma, with hyperplasia and, rarely, carcinoma accounting for the remainder
Many patients are asymptomatic and detected on incidental hypercalcaemia; classical symptoms are summarised as bones, stones, abdominal groans, and psychic moans
The biochemical hallmark is hypercalcaemia with an inappropriately non-suppressed or elevated parathyroid hormone level
Chronic disease can cause nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, osteoporosis or osteitis fibrosa cystica, peptic ulceration, and pancreatitis
Localisation before surgery combines neck ultrasound with sestamibi scintigraphy, and 4D-CT is useful when these are discordant or negative
Minimally invasive (focused) parathyroidectomy is favoured when a single adenoma is confidently localised, often guided by intraoperative parathyroid hormone measurement
Consider familial and syndromic disease (MEN 1, MEN 2A, familial hyperparathyroidism) in young patients or those with multigland involvement
reference.pathophysiology: A parathyroid adenoma is a benign clonal proliferation of chief cells that secretes parathyroid hormone autonomously, independent of the normal negative feedback from serum calcium. Excess PTH increases osteoclastic bone resorption, enhances renal tubular calcium reabsorption while promoting phosphate excretion, and stimulates renal activation of vitamin D, which raises intestinal calcium absorption. The net result is hypercalcaemia and hypophosphataemia. Sustained bone resorption reduces bone density, and the filtered calcium load promotes renal stone formation and, over time, renal impairment.
additionalDifferentials: Malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia (PTH-related peptide or bony metastases)
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney disease
Vitamin D intoxication or granulomatous disease (e.g. sarcoidosis)
additionalInvestigations: Serum calcium (corrected or ionised), phosphate, and intact PTH
24-hour urinary calcium to help exclude familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia
Vitamin D level and renal function assessment
Neck ultrasound and technetium-99m sestamibi scintigraphy for localisation
4D-CT or selective venous sampling in reoperative or non-localising cases
Bone density (DXA) scan and renal imaging for end-organ effects
redFlags: Severe hypercalcaemia with confusion, dehydration, arrhythmia, or hypercalcaemic crisis requiring urgent treatment
Very high calcium with a palpable neck mass or markedly elevated PTH raising suspicion of parathyroid carcinoma
Renal impairment or obstructing calculi from longstanding disease
Pathological fractures from advanced skeletal involvement
reference.prognosis: Surgical removal of a solitary adenoma is curative in the great majority, with normalisation of calcium and PTH and improvement in bone density and stone risk over time. Outcomes are excellent when a single gland is correctly identified; multigland disease or missed ectopic glands increases the risk of persistent or recurrent hyperparathyroidism.
pitfalls: Attributing hypercalcaemia to an adenoma without excluding familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, in whom surgery is inappropriate
Relying on a single localising study and missing an ectopic (mediastinal or intrathyroidal) gland
Overlooking four-gland hyperplasia and performing an inadequate focused exploration
Failing to recognise MEN syndromes, leading to incomplete treatment and missed associated tumours
Not monitoring for postoperative hypocalcaemia, including hungry bone syndrome after severe disease
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Offer parathyroidectomy, typically focused minimally invasive excision of the localised single adenoma, as the definitive curative treatment
Localise the adenoma preoperatively with neck ultrasound and technetium-99m sestamibi scintigraphy, adding 4D-CT when these are discordant or negative
Use intraoperative parathyroid hormone measurement to confirm biochemical cure before completing focused surgery
For patients unfit for or declining surgery, control hypercalcaemia with the calcimimetic cinacalcet and protect the skeleton with a bisphosphonate, alongside adequate hydration
Correct any coexisting vitamin D deficiency cautiously and encourage good fluid intake to reduce stone formation
Monitor postoperatively for hypocalcaemia, including hungry-bone syndrome, and for recurrent laryngeal nerve dysfunction
Undertake long-term surveillance of calcium, renal function and bone density, and screen for multigland or familial disease where features suggest it
